Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Shows Promise but Limited Real-World Healthcare Infection Surveillance

Artificial intelligence and automated tools can support multiple stages of healthcare-associated infection surveillance, yet relatively few systems have transitioned from retrospective evaluation into live hospital operations, according to a scoping review. The analysis examined how modern computational approaches assist infection prevention teams in tracking hospital-acquired conditions while evaluating their overall readiness for routine clinical implementation. Across the literature, automated methods proved particularly applicable for supporting case definitions, prioritizing records for clinical review, and generating candidate infection cases within supervised surveillance workflows.

The operational utility of any automated system depends heavily on the specific workflow stage at which its analytical output is deployed, the exact types of clinical data required for execution, and whether hospital personnel possess the capacity to review and act on generated alerts. Researchers aimed to map current implementations and systematically determine their practical readiness across healthcare environments.

To assess the current state of technology, investigators conducted a formal scoping review adhering to methodological guidance for scoping reviews and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. The investigative team systematically searched five academic databases for English-language publications released between January 2019 and April 2026. This comprehensive search identified 4,252 records for initial screening, from which reviewers selected 102 full-text reports for detailed assessment, ultimately incorporating 80 unique studies into the final analysis.

The study evaluation protocol categorized each included publication using prespecified workflow positions and implementation-readiness domains. To maintain rigorous evaluation standards, a second independent reviewer verified 16 key data fields across all 80 included studies.

Among clinical applications, surgical site infection detection emerged as the single most frequent target of automation, accounting for 38 of the 80 analyzed studies, or 47.5 percent of the literature. Within hospital operational workflows, investigators found that systems occupied three primary functional positions: providing case-definition support in 23 studies, assisting with triage or record prioritization in 20 studies, and performing candidate case generation in 13 studies.

Despite widespread technical interest, the scoping review revealed significant gaps between initial algorithmic development and practical bedside adoption. Fifty-one of the 80 studies remained restricted to retrospective offline evaluations, while 11 functioned strictly as early prototypes or proofs of concept. Only 9 publications described an active live pilot or genuine routine clinical deployment within a functioning healthcare environment, demonstrating that true operational integration remains rare across infection control departments.

External validation and system generalizability also appeared severely constrained across the reviewed evidence base. Only five studies reported external validation of their models, with three evaluating performance at a single external facility and merely two assessing tools across multiple external sites.

Operational governance and staffing impacts represented additional underreported domains in the available literature. Workload changes during active operational use were formally quantified in only two studies, and operational governance frameworks were explicitly specified in just two reports. While machine learning can extract evidence and prioritize chart reviews, the authors concluded that future prospective evaluations must rigorously establish real-world workflow utility, measure clinical workload, and define governance responsibilities and supervisory oversight across diverse clinical settings.

Subject of Research: Implementation readiness of artificial intelligence in healthcare-associated infection surveillance

Article Title: Artificial intelligence for healthcare-associated infection surveillance and control: a scoping review of evidence and implementation readiness

Article References: An, X., Jiang, N., & Ma, Y. (2026). Artificial intelligence for healthcare-associated infection surveillance and control: a scoping review of evidence and implementation readiness. BMC Infectious Diseases. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12879-026-14846-7

Keywords: artificial intelligence, healthcare-associated infections, infection surveillance, scoping review, surgical site infection, infection control, clinical automation, implementation science, case-definition support, triage prioritization, candidate generation, external validation, operational governance, health informatics, PRISMA-ScR

News Source: Kristina Jarvis. (November 12, 2026). Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Shows Promise but Limited Real-World Healthcare Infection Surveillance. Scienmag.
